newsitem.title: USA: China, U.S. join N. and S. Koreas for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: China, U.S. join N. and S. Koreas for peace talks.

text.p: North Korea on Tuesday opened talks with the United States, South Korea and China aimed at arranging negotiations toward a more secure peace than the one that ended the 1950-1953 Korean War.
Initial indications were that talks were proceeding well as the four parties held their first deliberations at Columbia University's School of Public and International Affairs.
"So far, so good," Chinese delegation head Chien Jian told reporters at the conclusion of the first session.
South Korean spokesman Ji Won Suh said that in the closed-door meeting North Korea expressed hope that "these preliminary talks will result in a fruitful conclusion."

Lead delegate Kim Gye Gwan explained that Pyongyang agreed to the meeting because "the four-party peace talks is regarded positively to establish a sustainable peace scheme on the Korean Peninsula," Suh said. A North Korean spokesman was not immediately available to confirm the remark.

The immediate goal of these "talks about talks" was to set a specific date, time and agenda for beginning substantive negotiations intended to replace the fraying Korean War armistice with a more permanent peace, presumably in a treaty.
If all this can be worked out this week, the substantive negotiations are expected to start sometime in September.

Suh said the negotiators accepted a Chinese suggestion to deal first with the easier issues such as date, level of representation and venue for the substantive talks and leave the thornier topic of agenda for last.
North Korea wanted to grapple with the agenda first but eventually sided with the majority, he told reporters.

Pyongyang's representative used his opening statement in the closed-door talks to stress that peace talks should not interfere in North Korea's domestic affairs and to argue that U.S. troops in South Korea should be a topic of discussion.
Suh interpreted this as blaming the Americans for tension on the heavily fortified Korean Peninsula but a U.S. official rejected any suggestion of trouble in the talks.
"This meeting is a positive development," said the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
"The fact of the matter is, there is a whole history that has to be overcome ... bad feelings do exist," and that is precisely why these peace talks were proposed, he said.

Since last March, the United States and South Korea have repeatedly tried to persuade the isolated Stalinist regime in Pyongyang to join the peace process proposed 17 months ago by the United States and South Korean presidents.
North Korea finally agreed in June. Tuesday's meeting marks a watershed because it includes China for the first time and is a step closer to actual negotiations.
"This is real progress. We have moved from a round table to a square table," chief U.S. delegate Charles Kartman told the delegations.

However, as they posed for a joint picture and handshake orchestrated by Kartman, the four delegation leaders responded with silence when asked by a reporter if they were confident they could agree on a date for the substantive negotiations.
The two-hour morning session was taken up largely with the four delegation chiefs making opening statements.

Suh, the South Korean spokesman, said North Korea argued that economic cooperation and confidence-building measures should be discussed between the two Koreas. "This is not very clear, but we have no objection to this," Suh said.

Suh quoted chief Chinese delegate Chen Jian as saying Beijing agreed to join the meeting because "it is historically important and we also think it is necessary to have a legal and systematic security to help build peace in this region."
China also believed a substitute for the armistice is required and backs reunification of the two Koreas, Suh said.
The U.S. side urged participants to make an "utmost effort" to ensure the talks are successful and pledged the United States would not be a bystander in this regard, he said.

The talks opened one day after North Korea, in an apparent goodwill gesture, turned over the remains of four U.S. servicemen missing from the Korean War and as international relief workers reported that a drought was compounding North Korea's severe food shortages.

A main obstacle to peace talks had been North Korea's demand for food aid to compensate for the famine caused by two years of severe rains and a system critics say is unable to meet the country's needs. Suh said food was not raised in the morning session, but could come up later.
